displayQuote: Laughter Would Be Bereaved If Snobbery Died

meta.title: Who really said "Laughter Would Be Bereaved If Snobbery Died"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Archbishop James Ussher — he died in 1656, before the word “snobbery” existed. Peter Ustinov said it, in The Observer, 13 March 1955.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Laughter Would Be Bereaved If Snobbery Died'?
meta.ogDescription: Not James Ussher. Peter Ustinov said it — The Observer, “Sayings of the Week”, 13 March 1955. The Ussher credit is an alphabetical slip.

answer.label: Not James Ussher — actually Peter Ustinov
answer.sourceLine: The line is Peter Ustinov’s, and its earliest known appearance is The Observer of 13 March 1955, in the “Sayings of the Week” list inside Pendennis’s “Table Talk” column, where it reads “Laughter would be bereaved if snobbery died. —Mr. Peter Ustinov.” Quote Investigator documents that printing ↗ and Wikiquote gives the same date independently ↗. The credit to Archbishop James Ussher is impossible on its face: he died in 1656. Note also that the form in wide circulation is the headline-style capitalisation of the research article that debunked it; the 1955 wording is an ordinary sentence.

source.excerpt: Laughter would be bereaved if snobbery died. —Mr. Peter Ustinov
trail: Quote Investigator’s article ↗ traces the earliest known appearance to The Observer of 13 March 1955, “Table Talk” by Pendennis, subsection “Sayings of the Week”, crediting Mr. Peter Ustinov. Its note records the citation as verified in the Guardian/Observer archive.

Wikiquote’s sourced Peter Ustinov page ↗ lists the line with the same source and date — “As quoted in The Observer (13 March 1955)” — which is an independent confirmation of the locator rather than a copy of the attribution.

The same QI article records the misattribution it debunks: The Times of London, 16 June 2011, Diary section, “The Last Word”, page 34, printed “Laughter would be bereft if snobbery died.” and credited it to “James Ussher, Irish prelate, 1581-1656”.

The dates settle it without needing any judgement about style: James Ussher ↗ lived from 4 January 1581 to 21 March 1656, while Peter Ustinov ↗ lived from 1921 to 2004 and the line is first seen in 1955.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording and the credit as The Observer printed them on 13 March 1955, transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the Guardian/Observer archive. The capitalised form people search for is the title of that research article, not a period wording.

source.rightsNote: The line was first published in The Observer on 13 March 1955 — well after the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff — and Ustinov died in 2004, so the quotation is in copyright. Short quotation for comment and criticism is the basis on which it is reproduced here. Note that the 1656 death of James Ussher, to whom it is often credited, would have made it public domain; the false credit and the rights status travel together.

author.heading: About Peter Ustinov
author.metaLine: 1921–2004 · British actor, writer, raconteur and humanitarian
author.bio: Sir Peter Alexander Ustinov (16 April 1921 – 28 March 2004) was a British actor, writer and humanitarian who won two Academy Awards for Best Supporting Actor, for Spartacus (1960) and Topkapi (1964). He was best known to the public as a raconteur, a fixture of television talk shows and lecture circuits for decades, which is exactly why a line of his turns up in a newspaper’s “Sayings of the Week” in 1955.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a quotation picking up the wrong name from the page layout rather than from any claim about who said it. Quote Investigator ↗ worked out the mechanism.

items.why: The Times of London ran the line on 16 June 2011 in “The Last Word” as “Laughter would be bereft if snobbery died.” — James Ussher, Irish prelate, 1581-1656. Ussher ↗ was the Church of Ireland Archbishop of Armagh, best known for dating the creation to 4004 BC. He died in 1656, roughly three centuries before the quotation appears.

In a quotation dictionary ordered by author, Ussher and Ustinov sit next to each other. QI’s explanation, credited to the correspondent who spotted the error, is that someone reading such a list took the name from the entry above the quotation instead of the one beside it. The same article notes that the Penguin Dictionary of Modern Quotations and the Oxford Dictionary of Humorous Quotations both carry it correctly under Ustinov.

QI raises a further possible source of confusion: the Anglo-Irish essayist Arland Ussher (1899–1980), who appears in quotation compilations with his own remark about humour, and whose entry a thematically arranged collection would have filed beside Ustinov’s. QI treats this as a plausible intermediate step, not an established one.

The 1955 Observer text reads bereaved. The Times’s 2011 misattributed version reads bereft. The two reference dictionaries QI checked both print “bereaved”, so the altered word travels with the wrong name.

misattribution.truthLine: Peter Ustinov is the author, first in print in The Observer on 13 March 1955 — as Quote Investigator documents ↗. James Ussher died in 1656 and had nothing to do with it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is a proper paradox rather than a put-down: snobbery is ridiculous, and comedy would miss it if it ever went away. It is very much Ustinov’s register — he made a career of mimicking the self-important without quite despising them — and in 1955 he was a thirty-three-year-old actor and playwright whose asides newspapers collected by the week.

Its afterlife is the more interesting part. A line about snobbery ended up being handed to a seventeenth-century archbishop because of where his name fell in an alphabet, which is roughly the error the quotation itself is making fun of: taking the label next to a thing for the thing.
detailsBody: The questioner who brought the problem to Quote Investigator noticed the anachronism in the vocabulary rather than the dates: QI reports her pointing out that the Oxford English Dictionary records “snob” from 1785, originally meaning a shoemaker or cobbler’s apprentice, and “snobbery” only from 1833 — both long after Ussher’s death. That reasoning is hers, by way of QI; quotle.info has not independently consulted the OED entries.

QI stops short of calling Ustinov the certain coiner, and so does this page. What is documented is that the earliest known printing is the 1955 Observer, that it credits him, and that two standard reference dictionaries have carried it under his name ever since. What is refuted, flatly, is James Ussher.
